newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonos still appeal, value seen in short end.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonos still appeal, value seen in short end.

text.p: Despite a fast run up since March, the Spanish bond market still looks attractive and many expect 10-year bonos to rise further ahead of the 1997 budget.
But a growing number of dealers have started to feel dizzy after the market reached record highs on Wednesday.
They recommend a more cautious approach, buying the less volatile short end of the curve which is likely to benefit from a possible fresh cut in key money rates.
"The Spanish market discounts a level of convergence toward the European single currency which I feel is exaggerated," said Alessandro Ceccaroni, director at UBS in London.
"Of course the short end is a less risky business," he said.
At 1400 GMT on Thursday the 10-year December bond future was up about 33 basis points at 104.22, while the less-traded three-year contract was up 27 bps at 99.09.
In anticipation of a tight 1997 budget set to be unveiled on September 27, the 10-year bond rose to record highs on Wednesday, pushing the yield down to 8.25 percent.
After the conservative Popular Power narrowly won a March election, the 10-year benchmark yielded 9.85 percent.

But any further gains at the long end of the curve will depend not only on the budget's approval but also on the convergence process toward a single European currency. Both factors could pose dangers in coming months, dealers said.
On Friday, EU finance ministers will start an informal meeting in Dublin.
"The coming months are the crucial ones for EMU. We can't rule out any surprise," one analyst said.
However, a fresh rate cut from the Bank of Spain seems more likely to the market than Spain joining a European Monetary Union from the start and that should support the short end of the yield curve.
"If the budget draft will be considered tight enough, the Bank of Spain could cut its official rate as early as October 3 by at least 25 bp," said a dealer, who declined to be named.

On Wednesday, Spanish central bank governor Luis Angel Rojo said the approval of a strict 1997 budget would increase the scope for manoeuvre in monetary policy. Since January 1996, the central bank cut its official rate five times from 9.0 percent to 7.25 percent.
The Mibor contract on 90-day interbank deposits was trading in the afternoon at 93.25, one point over Wednesday's close. Dealers said a rate cut has already been partly priced in.
On Thursday, a note to clients of Bank of America Madrid advised them not to "reduce the exposure or leave the Spanish bond market from a strategic point of view."
But the bank recommended staying short 10-year bonds in the next two weeks.
"In general, five-year bonds seem to offer a greater value, better than the 10-year bonds," said Luis Martin, chief dealer at Deutsche Bank in Madrid.
But others still prefer riskier bets.
"I do still believe Spain will take part, sooner or later, in European Monetary Union and I am convinced the 10-year Spanish bond will break the 8.25 percent level," a dealer said.
He recommened buying from seven years out.
The 10.15 percent 10-year benchmark was trading at 111.55-65 from 111.49 at Wednesday's close with the yield unchanged at 8.30 percent.
-- Madrid Newsroom +341 - 585.2152
